Some analysts believe Russia was seeking to demonstrate its commitment to its alliance with North Korea. According to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff, a Russian strategic bomber formation entered the KADIZ around 7:40 am on Tuesday and flew south toward Ulleung Island. By 7:52 am, the aircraft had approached within 13 nautical miles of the island and just 1 nautical mile from the boundary of Korean airspace. Another two or three seconds of flight would have taken them into Korean airspace. The South Korean military responded by scrambling several F-15K fighter jets. Russia’s Defense Ministry identified the aircraft flying over the East Sea that day as Tu-160 strategic bombers conducting a scheduled flight over international waters, according to Russia’s TASS news agency. The flight lasted approximately 10 hours, with the bombers escorted by Su-35S and Su-30SM fighter jets from the Russian Aerospace Forces. The Russian Defense Ministry said its aircraft strictly comply with international rules on the use of airspace in all flights. The Tu-160 is a supersonic long-range strategic bomber capable of carrying nuclear missiles, with a maximum range of over 12,000 kilometers. Its all-white paint scheme has earned it the moniker “White Swan.” The formation that entered KADIZ consisted of four aircraft: two Tu-160 bombers with an escort of one Su-35S and one Su-30SM fighter. Korea’s Defense Ministry summoned the Russian defense attaché, a colonel in the air force, to lodge a protest. The Foreign Ministry did not summon the Russian ambassador but expressed regret through diplomatic channels and urged Moscow to ensure that such an incident is not repeated. Russia’s Foreign Ministry, meanwhile, announced that Korean Ambassador to Russia Lee Sok-bae had met with Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko to discuss pressing issues.
https://www.hani.co.kr/arti/english_edit.paragraph_2: The incident was unusual in several respects. For one thing, the nuclear-capable Tu-160 strategic bomber has never before made an appearance over the East Sea (also called the Sea of Japan). Known as the world’s largest supersonic strategic bomber, the Tu-160 can carry air-launched cruise missiles fitted with nuclear warheads and reach speeds of around Mach 2. Russia gave North Korean leader Kim Jong-un a tour of its strategic bombers, including the Tu-160, during his visit to Vladivostok in September 2023. Russia has sent Tu-95MS bombers into the KADIZ on multiple previous occasions. But on this occasion, it sent the supersonic Tu-160 to the very edge of South Korean airspace, cranking up the pressure on Seoul. Russian military aircraft have recently passed through the KADIZ on their way to Japan’s air defense identification zone. This time, however, the Russian aircraft did not continue toward Japan after narrowly skirting South Korean airspace over Ulleung Island, suggesting that the operation was aimed specifically at South Korea. Experts believe Russia’s primary objective was to demonstrate to North Korea that it is fulfilling its obligations under their Treaty on Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, while also using the show of force to put pressure on the South Korean government. Russia and North Korea’s treaty, signed in June 2024, pledges mutual military assistance. Russian President Vladimir Putin emphasized the two countries’ brotherhood in arms and their commitment to the treaty in a meeting with Jo Yong-won, a senior official in North Korea’s ruling party, on Nov. 16. “The fact that Russia’s strategic bombers only brushed by South Korea this time without continuing on to Japan suggests that the operation was intended to send a message to both South and North Korea,” said Doo Jin-ho, a visiting research fellow at Kyungnam University’s Institute for Far Eastern Studies. “North Korea has sent combat troops to Russia, but Russia hadn’t previously rotated strategic assets into the region. It apparently wanted to show the North that it’s honoring its defense commitments,” Doo said. Lee Byong-chul, a professor at the same institute, said that Russia was “visibly demonstrating its commitment to defending North Korea under their bilateral treaty while also providing deterrence against the South Korea-US alliance and signaling that it could intervene in a contingency on the Korean Peninsula.” “Just as the US deploys strategic weapons to the Korean Peninsula under its mutual defense treaty with South Korea, Russia may continue deploying strategic weapons in the future as North Korea’s military backer,” Lee said.
